amendments.why: Rule 41's articleless-attributive sentence gives the supplied relative to the attributive, and its limit lists three marks that identify a predication instead: a subject or resumptive pronoun, a coordinated finite clause under the same relative, and a same-shaped clause rendered as a main clause elsewhere in the passage. None of the three reaches PRO.20.7, `מִתְהַלֵּךְ בְּתֻמּוֹ צַדִּיק` → *A righteous man that walketh in his integrity*, where the participle is fronted before the noun with its own prepositional phrase between them and the ASV has subordinated a predication rather than rendered an attributive. Word order is what decides it, and it is a fact about the source rather than about the translation: a Hebrew attributive follows its noun. The chapter supplies the minimal pair — PRO.20.7 fronted with the *that* `added`, PRO.20.8 `מֶלֶךְ יוֹשֵׁב` following with the *that* on the participle — and PRO.20.1 and PRO.20.26 read two further fronted participles as predicates. Without this the limit is under-determined and the next chapter will hand the relative to a fronted predicate, so the fourth mark is added where the three already stand, with a rider excluding a participle in construct on the following noun, which rules 46 and 19 already govern.
amendments.rule: The **substantival article** — `הַ` on a participle or adjective used as a noun — takes the pronoun the ASV supplies to make it substantival, and heads on that pronoun rather than on the relative that follows it. `הָרַע` → *that which was evil* is the article with *that which*, headed on *that*; `הָעֹשֶׂה` → *him that doeth* is the article with *him that*, headed on *him*. The supplied pronoun is the article's own rendering and is never `added`. The predicate word keeps its own English, including any copula the ASV supplies, which stays with it under rule 20: in *that which is right*, *is* and *right* belong to the adjective and only *that which* belongs to the article. **An attributive article the ASV renders by a relative goes the same way.** Where `הַ` stands on a participle or adjective modifying an explicit noun and the ASV writes a relative instead of a *the* — `אֹיְבֶיךָ הַקָּמִים עָלֶיךָ` → *thine enemies that rise up against thee*, `הָאִישׁ הָרַךְ` → *The man that is tender*, `הַכְּתוּבִים` → *that are written*, `הַכֹּהֵן הַמְחַטֵּא` → *The priest that offereth* — the article takes that relative and heads on it, while the participle or adjective keeps its own English together with any supplied copula, exactly as above. **But read where the ASV has put the attributive before reaching for that sentence.** Where it renders the attributive prenominally instead, no relative stands before the attributive's own word and rule 47 governs the count: the phrase's single *the* is the first article's and the agreement article is `unrepresented`, as `הַכֹּהֵן הַמָּשִׁיחַ` → *the anointed priest* is. **A demonstrative, possessive or quantifying determiner the ASV writes in the article's place goes the same way, whatever the article stands on.** Where the ASV writes no *the* for the phrase but a *this*, *that*, *these*, *those*, a possessive *his*, *her*, *thy*, *thine*, or a quantifier such as *any* or *every*, standing where the phrase's *the* would stand — `הַזִּמָּה` → *this lewdness*, `הַגְּדֹלוֹת` → *thine elder*, `הַבֶּגֶד` → *any garment* — that word is what the ASV has written for the article: the article takes it and heads on it, and it is neither `added` nor a reason to mark the article `unrepresented`. A quantifying determiner is read on exactly the terms of the others and is not left to the noun under rule 15: that rule gives a supplied *any* to the nominal expression only where no determiner morpheme stands before the word it determines, and an article standing on that word is such a morpheme. **Read that as no *the* standing before the article's own word, not as no *the* anywhere in the phrase.** Where the article sits on the *nomen rectum* of a construct chain and the ASV writes a *the* before the construct and a demonstrative or possessive before the rectum's own word, rule 29's arthrous case governs the count: nothing is fronted, the article takes the determiner standing before its own word, and the construct takes the supplied *the*. `יְמֵי הַמִּשְׁתֶּה` → *the days of* ***their*** *feasting* gives *their* to the article and *the days* to the construct, exactly as `שְׂדֵה הָעִיר` → *the fields of the city* gives the second *the* to the article there. Do not mark such an article `unrepresented` and the determiner `added` under rule 18's closing sentence: that sentence governs a supplied possessive with no determiner morpheme standing before the word it determines, and here one does. **But only where no other morpheme licenses that determiner.** A pronominal suffix standing in the same phrase is rendered by a possessive of its own under rule 18, a `כֹּל` standing on the noun is itself what an *any* or an *every* renders under rule 15, an `אֶחָד` standing in the phrase is itself what a distributive *each* or *every* renders, and a demonstrative pronoun standing in the phrase is itself what a written *this*, *that*, *these* or *those* renders; where the ASV writes one determiner for the whole phrase that morpheme takes it and the article is `unrepresented`: `אֲחוֹתֵךְ הַגְּדוֹלָה` → *thine elder sister* gives *thine* to the suffix on `אָחוֹת` and leaves the article nothing, while `אֲחוֹתַיִךְ הַגְּדֹלוֹת` → *thy sisters, thine elder sisters* writes a determiner for each and the article takes the second; so too `אֲחִיהֶם הַבְּכוֹר` → *their eldest brother's*, where the suffix takes *their* and the article has nothing, and `הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא` → *that place*, where `הוּא` takes the written *that* while the noun's article and the agreement article beside it are both `unrepresented` under rule 47. **And the morpheme that licenses the determiner need not stand inside the noun phrase.** What the preceding sentences ask is which morpheme the written determiner answers to, so read the clause rather than the phrase's edges: where a dative or possessive `לְ` with a pronominal suffix stands beside the noun and the ASV recasts it as a possessive determiner on that noun, the suffix is what the determiner realizes under rules 18 and 40, the `לְ` is `unrepresented` under rule 40, and the article is `unrepresented` exactly as it is beside a suffix written on the noun itself. `וַיְהִי לָהֶם הַגְּבוּל` → *And* ***their*** *border was* gives *their* to the suffix, *was* to `הָיָה` under rule 43, and nothing to either the preposition or the article. Do not hand such a determiner to the article on the ground that the suffix stands outside the phrase: that would leave the morpheme the ASV wrote the word for holding nothing, against rules 2 and 18. Count the determiners and read which word each stands before, as rule 29 counts the ASV's *the*s. **The `אֶחָד` case is counted on exactly those terms, and it turns on the one word the ASV wrote rather than on where that word stands.** A distributive determiner stands precisely where the phrase's *the* would stand, so the preceding sentences alone would hand it to the article; the numeral takes it because the numeral is itself what the word says. Where the ASV writes one such determiner, it is the numeral's and every article in the phrase — the noun's own and the agreement article on the numeral alike — is `unrepresented`: `לַפָּר הָאֶחָד` → *for* ***each*** *bullock* and `לַכֶּבֶשׂ הָאֶחָד` → *for* ***every*** *lamb*. Where it instead writes a *the* before the noun and an *one* for the numeral, two determiners are written and each morpheme takes the one standing before its own word: `לָאַיִל הָאֶחָד` → *for* ***the one*** *ram* gives *the* to the noun's article and *one* to the numeral, the agreement article still `unrepresented` under rule 47. One verse may write both shapes, and NUM.28.12 and NUM.28.28 do. The corpus aligns `אֶחָד` to *each* in 18 units, to *every* in four and to *every one* in five, so a numeral standing in the phrase is a morpheme that licenses such a determiner; the article's own units of *every* are the case this sentence excludes, where no such numeral stands. **And a determiner another morpheme licenses is still a determiner standing before the article's own word.** The count above is unchanged where the preceding sentences have left the article with nothing: still nothing is fronted, and where such a phrase is the *nomen rectum* of a construct chain the construct takes a supplied *the* of its own. `שֵׁם הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא` → *the name of that place* gives *the name* to the construct, *that* to the demonstrative pronoun, and nothing to either article. Do not read the article's silence as an anarthrous rendering and hand the construct's *the* back to it as a fronted determiner: what forces fronting under rule 29 is a rectum the ASV renders with no determiner at all — `לֻחֹת הָאֲבָנִים` → *the two tables of stone* — and a rectum whose own word carries a *this*, a *that* or a possessive is not that, whichever morpheme in the phrase the word answers to. Read what stands before the rectum's word, not which morpheme was left with nothing. Read what the ASV writes for the article and let that decide which rule governs: a bare *the* is rule 15's ordinary attributive article, a relative or a supplied pronoun is this rule's, a demonstrative, possessive or quantifying determiner is this rule's too, and where the ASV writes none of them the article is `unrepresented` under rule 29. Where coordinated attributives share a single written relative, the first article takes it and the rest are `unrepresented` under rules 22 and 47. **An articleless attributive that the ASV recasts as a relative clause keeps the supplied relative with the attributive itself.** Where an adjective or participle without an article modifies an explicit noun and the ASV writes a relative frame — `אֲדָמָה טְמֵאָה` → *a land that is unclean* — the attributive takes the relative together with its own English and any copula rule 20 supplies, headed on the word carrying its lexeme. The relative realizes the Hebrew attributive relation and is not `added`; rule 55's supplied clause subordinator is a different construction. **But read whether the Hebrew writes an attributive or a predication before reaching for that sentence.** What it governs is an adjective or participle standing with the noun it modifies inside one nominal expression, as `אֲדָמָה טְמֵאָה` is. Where the adjective or participle is instead the predicate of a verbless clause and the ASV subordinates that clause to the noun standing as its subject, the English relative subordinates a clause rather than realizing an attributive relation, so rules 46 and 55 govern it: the relative answers to no morpheme and is its own `added` unit, while the copula and the predicate's own English stay with the adjective or participle under rule 20. `דּוֹר טָהוֹר בְּעֵינָיו` → *a generation* ***that*** *are pure in their own eyes* and `לַיִשׁ גִּבּוֹר בַּבְּהֵמָה` → *The lion,* ***which*** *is mightiest among beasts* both leave the relative `added` and give *are pure* and *is mightiest* to the adjective. Read the Hebrew clause rather than the English noun phrase the ASV has built around it, since a translation that subordinates a predication writes exactly what an attributive relation writes. Four things mark a predication. A subject or resumptive pronoun standing in the clause is one, as the `הֵם` of `אַרְבָּעָה הֵם קְטַנֵּי־אָרֶץ` → *four things* ***which*** *are little upon the earth* is. A further finite clause coordinated under the same English relative is another, since no attributive frame carries one. A clause of the same shape elsewhere in the passage that the ASV renders as a main clause with a copula is the third, as `הַנְּמָלִים עַם לֹא־עָז` → *The ants are a people not strong* stands beside the `לַיִשׁ גִּבּוֹר` above. **And the Hebrew's own word order is the fourth, which is the plainest of them.** An attributive follows the noun it modifies, so a participle or adjective standing before the noun the ASV has made the head of its English noun phrase is that clause's predicate and not an attributive, whatever order the English writes: `מִתְהַלֵּךְ בְּתֻמּוֹ צַדִּיק` → *A righteous man* ***that*** *walketh in his integrity* opens with the participle and stands the participle's own prepositional phrase between it and the noun, so the *that* is `added` and the participle keeps only its own *walketh*, while `מֶלֶךְ יוֹשֵׁב עַל־כִּסֵּא דִין` → *A king* ***that*** *sitteth on the throne of judgment* writes the participle after its noun and the preceding sentence governs. Read the order of the source tokens rather than the ASV's, since a translation that subordinates a fronted predicate writes exactly what an attributive writes, and one chapter may write both shapes, as PRO.20.7 and PRO.20.8 do; a fronted participle the ASV renders as a finite predicate of its own — `מְזָרֶה רְשָׁעִים מֶלֶךְ חָכָם` → *A wise king winnoweth the wicked* — is the same shape read without a relative and needs nothing placed. But read what the fronted word governs before applying this mark: a participle in construct on the noun that follows it is a substantive with its own dependent, and rules 46 and 19 govern it, as `יִרְאֵי יְהֵוָה` → *them that feared Jehovah* is. Where none of these four is present and the Hebrew writes an attributive inside a nominal expression, the preceding sentence governs as before.

conventions: Distributive repetition in this chapter (`אֶבֶן וָאֶבֶן`, `אֵיפָה וְאֵיפָה`, PRO.20.10 and PRO.20.23) is read under rule 22's distributive paragraph: the first occurrence takes the noun's own English together with the ASV's supplied *Diverse* under rule 15, and the repetition's waw and its second noun are each their own `unrepresented` unit. The chapter's written *and* is then placed by the pair of items it stands between, as rule 42 directs, and not by preferring a position: PRO.20.23 writes a waw at the boundary between the two coordinated nominals and that waw takes it, while PRO.20.10 sets the weights pair beside the measures pair with no conjunction at that boundary, so its *and* is `added` under rule 14's closing sentence and both of its waws are unrepresented. The two verses look inconsistent in English and are not.

In a verbless comparison the construction-supplied copula goes to the predicate nominal and never to the comparative, whether the comparison is carried by a written `כְ` — PRO.20.2 `נַהַם כַּכְּפִיר אֵימַת מֶלֶךְ` → *is as the roaring*, with *is the roaring* on `נַהַם` and the bare *as* on the `כְ` — or by a supplied *like*, as PRO.20.5 `מַיִם עֲמֻקִּים` → *is like deep water* puts both words on `מַיִם` under rules 20 and 33. The Hebrew, not the English word order, says which side is the predicate: the comparative phrase is an adjunct inside the predicate, which is the carve-out rule 49's closing paragraph makes. Where the ASV then writes a further English relation before the compared noun and the `כְ` has already been spent on *as*, that word joins the compared noun's unit rather than returning to the preposition, which is not a home for a second word — PRO.20.2 `כְּפִיר` → *of a lion* (rules 33, 52).

amended.text: The **substantival article** — `הַ` on a participle or adjective used as a noun — takes the pronoun the ASV supplies to make it substantival, and heads on that pronoun rather than on the relative that follows it. `הָרַע` → *that which was evil* is the article with *that which*, headed on *that*; `הָעֹשֶׂה` → *him that doeth* is the article with *him that*, headed on *him*. The supplied pronoun is the article's own rendering and is never `added`. The predicate word keeps its own English, including any copula the ASV supplies, which stays with it under rule 20: in *that which is right*, *is* and *right* belong to the adjective and only *that which* belongs to the article. **An attributive article the ASV renders by a relative goes the same way.** Where `הַ` stands on a participle or adjective modifying an explicit noun and the ASV writes a relative instead of a *the* — `אֹיְבֶיךָ הַקָּמִים עָלֶיךָ` → *thine enemies that rise up against thee*, `הָאִישׁ הָרַךְ` → *The man that is tender*, `הַכְּתוּבִים` → *that are written*, `הַכֹּהֵן הַמְחַטֵּא` → *The priest that offereth* — the article takes that relative and heads on it, while the participle or adjective keeps its own English together with any supplied copula, exactly as above. **But read where the ASV has put the attributive before reaching for that sentence.** Where it renders the attributive prenominally instead, no relative stands before the attributive's own word and rule 47 governs the count: the phrase's single *the* is the first article's and the agreement article is `unrepresented`, as `הַכֹּהֵן הַמָּשִׁיחַ` → *the anointed priest* is. **A demonstrative, possessive or quantifying determiner the ASV writes in the article's place goes the same way, whatever the article stands on.** Where the ASV writes no *the* for the phrase but a *this*, *that*, *these*, *those*, a possessive *his*, *her*, *thy*, *thine*, or a quantifier such as *any* or *every*, standing where the phrase's *the* would stand — `הַזִּמָּה` → *this lewdness*, `הַגְּדֹלוֹת` → *thine elder*, `הַבֶּגֶד` → *any garment* — that word is what the ASV has written for the article: the article takes it and heads on it, and it is neither `added` nor a reason to mark the article `unrepresented`. A quantifying determiner is read on exactly the terms of the others and is not left to the noun under rule 15: that rule gives a supplied *any* to the nominal expression only where no determiner morpheme stands before the word it determines, and an article standing on that word is such a morpheme. **Read that as no *the* standing before the article's own word, not as no *the* anywhere in the phrase.** Where the article sits on the *nomen rectum* of a construct chain and the ASV writes a *the* before the construct and a demonstrative or possessive before the rectum's own word, rule 29's arthrous case governs the count: nothing is fronted, the article takes the determiner standing before its own word, and the construct takes the supplied *the*. `יְמֵי הַמִּשְׁתֶּה` → *the days of* ***their*** *feasting* gives *their* to the article and *the days* to the construct, exactly as `שְׂדֵה הָעִיר` → *the fields of the city* gives the second *the* to the article there. Do not mark such an article `unrepresented` and the determiner `added` under rule 18's closing sentence: that sentence governs a supplied possessive with no determiner morpheme standing before the word it determines, and here one does. **But only where no other morpheme licenses that determiner.** A pronominal suffix standing in the same phrase is rendered by a possessive of its own under rule 18, a `כֹּל` standing on the noun is itself what an *any* or an *every* renders under rule 15, an `אֶחָד` standing in the phrase is itself what a distributive *each* or *every* renders, and a demonstrative pronoun standing in the phrase is itself what a written *this*, *that*, *these* or *those* renders; where the ASV writes one determiner for the whole phrase that morpheme takes it and the article is `unrepresented`: `אֲחוֹתֵךְ הַגְּדוֹלָה` → *thine elder sister* gives *thine* to the suffix on `אָחוֹת` and leaves the article nothing, while `אֲחוֹתַיִךְ הַגְּדֹלוֹת` → *thy sisters, thine elder sisters* writes a determiner for each and the article takes the second; so too `אֲחִיהֶם הַבְּכוֹר` → *their eldest brother's*, where the suffix takes *their* and the article has nothing, and `הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא` → *that place*, where `הוּא` takes the written *that* while the noun's article and the agreement article beside it are both `unrepresented` under rule 47. **And the morpheme that licenses the determiner need not stand inside the noun phrase.** What the preceding sentences ask is which morpheme the written determiner answers to, so read the clause rather than the phrase's edges: where a dative or possessive `לְ` with a pronominal suffix stands beside the noun and the ASV recasts it as a possessive determiner on that noun, the suffix is what the determiner realizes under rules 18 and 40, the `לְ` is `unrepresented` under rule 40, and the article is `unrepresented` exactly as it is beside a suffix written on the noun itself. `וַיְהִי לָהֶם הַגְּבוּל` → *And* ***their*** *border was* gives *their* to the suffix, *was* to `הָיָה` under rule 43, and nothing to either the preposition or the article. Do not hand such a determiner to the article on the ground that the suffix stands outside the phrase: that would leave the morpheme the ASV wrote the word for holding nothing, against rules 2 and 18. Count the determiners and read which word each stands before, as rule 29 counts the ASV's *the*s. **The `אֶחָד` case is counted on exactly those terms, and it turns on the one word the ASV wrote rather than on where that word stands.** A distributive determiner stands precisely where the phrase's *the* would stand, so the preceding sentences alone would hand it to the article; the numeral takes it because the numeral is itself what the word says. Where the ASV writes one such determiner, it is the numeral's and every article in the phrase — the noun's own and the agreement article on the numeral alike — is `unrepresented`: `לַפָּר הָאֶחָד` → *for* ***each*** *bullock* and `לַכֶּבֶשׂ הָאֶחָד` → *for* ***every*** *lamb*. Where it instead writes a *the* before the noun and an *one* for the numeral, two determiners are written and each morpheme takes the one standing before its own word: `לָאַיִל הָאֶחָד` → *for* ***the one*** *ram* gives *the* to the noun's article and *one* to the numeral, the agreement article still `unrepresented` under rule 47. One verse may write both shapes, and NUM.28.12 and NUM.28.28 do. The corpus aligns `אֶחָד` to *each* in 18 units, to *every* in four and to *every one* in five, so a numeral standing in the phrase is a morpheme that licenses such a determiner; the article's own units of *every* are the case this sentence excludes, where no such numeral stands. **And a determiner another morpheme licenses is still a determiner standing before the article's own word.** The count above is unchanged where the preceding sentences have left the article with nothing: still nothing is fronted, and where such a phrase is the *nomen rectum* of a construct chain the construct takes a supplied *the* of its own. `שֵׁם הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא` → *the name of that place* gives *the name* to the construct, *that* to the demonstrative pronoun, and nothing to either article. Do not read the article's silence as an anarthrous rendering and hand the construct's *the* back to it as a fronted determiner: what forces fronting under rule 29 is a rectum the ASV renders with no determiner at all — `לֻחֹת הָאֲבָנִים` → *the two tables of stone* — and a rectum whose own word carries a *this*, a *that* or a possessive is not that, whichever morpheme in the phrase the word answers to. Read what stands before the rectum's word, not which morpheme was left with nothing. Read what the ASV writes for the article and let that decide which rule governs: a bare *the* is rule 15's ordinary attributive article, a relative or a supplied pronoun is this rule's, a demonstrative, possessive or quantifying determiner is this rule's too, and where the ASV writes none of them the article is `unrepresented` under rule 29. Where coordinated attributives share a single written relative, the first article takes it and the rest are `unrepresented` under rules 22 and 47. **An articleless attributive that the ASV recasts as a relative clause keeps the supplied relative with the attributive itself.** Where an adjective or participle without an article modifies an explicit noun and the ASV writes a relative frame — `אֲדָמָה טְמֵאָה` → *a land that is unclean* — the attributive takes the relative together with its own English and any copula rule 20 supplies, headed on the word carrying its lexeme. The relative realizes the Hebrew attributive relation and is not `added`; rule 55's supplied clause subordinator is a different construction. **But read whether the Hebrew writes an attributive or a predication before reaching for that sentence.** What it governs is an adjective or participle standing with the noun it modifies inside one nominal expression, as `אֲדָמָה טְמֵאָה` is. Where the adjective or participle is instead the predicate of a verbless clause and the ASV subordinates that clause to the noun standing as its subject, the English relative subordinates a clause rather than realizing an attributive relation, so rules 46 and 55 govern it: the relative answers to no morpheme and is its own `added` unit, while the copula and the predicate's own English stay with the adjective or participle under rule 20. `דּוֹר טָהוֹר בְּעֵינָיו` → *a generation* ***that*** *are pure in their own eyes* and `לַיִשׁ גִּבּוֹר בַּבְּהֵמָה` → *The lion,* ***which*** *is mightiest among beasts* both leave the relative `added` and give *are pure* and *is mightiest* to the adjective. Read the Hebrew clause rather than the English noun phrase the ASV has built around it, since a translation that subordinates a predication writes exactly what an attributive relation writes. Four things mark a predication. A subject or resumptive pronoun standing in the clause is one, as the `הֵם` of `אַרְבָּעָה הֵם קְטַנֵּי־אָרֶץ` → *four things* ***which*** *are little upon the earth* is. A further finite clause coordinated under the same English relative is another, since no attributive frame carries one. A clause of the same shape elsewhere in the passage that the ASV renders as a main clause with a copula is the third, as `הַנְּמָלִים עַם לֹא־עָז` → *The ants are a people not strong* stands beside the `לַיִשׁ גִּבּוֹר` above. **And the Hebrew's own word order is the fourth, which is the plainest of them.** An attributive follows the noun it modifies, so a participle or adjective standing before the noun the ASV has made the head of its English noun phrase is that clause's predicate and not an attributive, whatever order the English writes: `מִתְהַלֵּךְ בְּתֻמּוֹ צַדִּיק` → *A righteous man* ***that*** *walketh in his integrity* opens with the participle and stands the participle's own prepositional phrase between it and the noun, so the *that* is `added` and the participle keeps only its own *walketh*, while `מֶלֶךְ יוֹשֵׁב עַל־כִּסֵּא דִין` → *A king* ***that*** *sitteth on the throne of judgment* writes the participle after its noun and the preceding sentence governs. Read the order of the source tokens rather than the ASV's, since a translation that subordinates a fronted predicate writes exactly what an attributive writes, and one chapter may write both shapes, as PRO.20.7 and PRO.20.8 do; a fronted participle the ASV renders as a finite predicate of its own — `מְזָרֶה רְשָׁעִים מֶלֶךְ חָכָם` → *A wise king winnoweth the wicked* — is the same shape read without a relative and needs nothing placed. But read what the fronted word governs before applying this mark: a participle in construct on the noun that follows it is a substantive with its own dependent, and rules 46 and 19 govern it, as `יִרְאֵי יְהֵוָה` → *them that feared Jehovah* is. Where none of these four is present and the Hebrew writes an attributive inside a nominal expression, the preceding sentence governs as before.
amended.why: Rule 41's articleless-attributive sentence gives the supplied relative to the attributive, and its limit lists three marks that identify a predication instead: a subject or resumptive pronoun, a coordinated finite clause under the same relative, and a same-shaped clause rendered as a main clause elsewhere in the passage. None of the three reaches PRO.20.7, `מִתְהַלֵּךְ בְּתֻמּוֹ צַדִּיק` → *A righteous man that walketh in his integrity*, where the participle is fronted before the noun with its own prepositional phrase between them and the ASV has subordinated a predication rather than rendered an attributive. Word order is what decides it, and it is a fact about the source rather than about the translation: a Hebrew attributive follows its noun. The chapter supplies the minimal pair — PRO.20.7 fronted with the *that* `added`, PRO.20.8 `מֶלֶךְ יוֹשֵׁב` following with the *that* on the participle — and PRO.20.1 and PRO.20.26 read two further fronted participles as predicates. Without this the limit is under-determined and the next chapter will hand the relative to a fronted predicate, so the fourth mark is added where the three already stand, with a rider excluding a participle in construct on the following noun, which rules 46 and 19 already govern.

report: Checked all 29 candidate lemma groups end to end, and read the dump for added-unit splits the lemma table cannot see. Every multi-treatment bucket is the ASV rendering one morpheme differently in a context the source licenses: the waw takes whichever connective the ASV wrote (And, But, Therefore, or, then, but when), and the assimilated article is aligned in PRO.20.21 (*at the beginning*) but unrepresented in PRO.20.2, .3, .4, .17 and .28, in each case exactly where the ASV writes *a* or nothing before the article's own word (rules 12, 29). No cross-verse split was found, so patches is empty.

The chapter's one substantive judgment is the PRO.20.7 / PRO.20.8 pair, and it is source-licensed rather than a split. In 20.7 the participle is fronted with its own prepositional phrase standing between it and the noun, so the colon is a predication the ASV subordinated and the supplied *that* is `added`; in 20.8 the participle follows its noun, so rule 41's articleless attributive governs and the *that* is the participle's. PRO.20.1 (fronted participle rendered *strong drink a brawler*) and PRO.20.26 (fronted participle rendered *A wise king winnoweth the wicked*) corroborate the fronted-participle-is-predicate reading inside the same chapter. Rule 41 names three marks of a predication and none of them reaches word order, so this is returned as an amendment adding a fourth.

The distributive repetition of weight-and-weight / measure-and-measure is analysed identically in PRO.20.10 and PRO.20.23 under rule 22's distributive paragraph: first occurrence takes the noun with the supplied *Diverse*, the repetition's waw and second noun go unrepresented. The one difference between the verses — the single written *and* is `added` in .10 and the waw's in .23 — is licensed by the source, since .23 writes a waw at the group boundary (s006) while .10 juxtaposes the two pairs asyndetically. Recorded as a convention, because a reader comparing the two verses would otherwise read it as an inconsistency.

Also checked and found consistent: rule 31 head choices (the class-noun tie-break puts *young men* and *old men* on *men*, while *strong drink*, *hoary head* and *high*-type phrases head on the modifier because the ASV never writes those class nouns alone for those lemmas here); rule 33's closing paragraph placing the *with* of *be satisfied with bread* (20.13) and *be filled with gravel* (20.17) on the predicate; rule 20's supplied dummy *It* marked `added` in 20.3, 20.14 (twice) and 20.25 (twice) with the copula always on the predicate; and rule 40's silenced prepositions in 20.14, 20.22 and 20.30.

BSB disagreements: all ten are documented convention differences, and none is a genuine error. PRO.20.1 (article on `הַיַּיִן` where the ASV writes bare *Wine*) is rule 29. PRO.20.10 and PRO.20.23 (two waws and three repeated nouns) are rule 22's distributive repetition, which BSB attaches to its own phrase. PRO.20.14 `לְ`, PRO.20.22 `לְ` and PRO.20.30 `בְּ` are rule 40 recastings that leave the preposition no English word — the ethical dative of *is gone his way*, the dative before the bare object of *save thee*, and the promoted object of *cleanse away evil*. No accepted edge was changed.
